Question 1 [15 marks]

(a) A mammary gland cell stimulated to secrete large amounts of a glycoprotein develops nucleoli that are larger and more darkly stained than those of an unstimulated cell of the same type. Explain why this change has to happen before the cell can secrete more glycoprotein. [6]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Why enlarged nucleoli must precede an increase in glycoprotein secretion. [6]

1. The nucleolus contains the genes coding for rRNA and is the site of rRNA synthesis / transcription of rRNA.

2. Larger, more darkly stained nucleoli mean more rRNA is being transcribed.

3. In the nucleolus, rRNA assembles with ribosomal proteins to form the large and the small ribosomal subunits, which are unequal in size.

4. The subunits leave the nucleus through the nuclear pores and assemble on mRNA in the cytoplasm to form a functional ribosome.

5. More ribosomes allow a higher rate of translation / protein synthesis.

6. The glycoprotein is secreted, so it is translated on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and more ribosomes on the rough ER means more glycoprotein made per unit time.

Gap closed: a nucleolus count earns nothing on its own. The chain is more nucleoli → more rRNA → more ribosomes → higher rate of protein synthesis.

Gap closed: the two ribosomal subunits are unequal, one large, one small.

(b) Two vesicles pinch off the trans face of the Golgi apparatus in that cell: one becomes a lysosome, the other carries the glycoprotein to the cell surface membrane and releases it outside. Identify the single membrane property both departures and the later arrival depend on, and state what happens to the total area of the cell surface membrane in each case. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The one membrane property behind budding, fusion and exocytosis, and the effect of each on cell surface membrane area. [5]

1. The property is fluidity / lateral movement of phospholipids within their own monolayer, because the phospholipids are held only by weak hydrophobic interactions between their hydrocarbon tails, which are easily broken and re-formed.

2. Fluidity allows the Golgi membrane to bend and pinch off a vesicle, and allows a vesicle membrane to fuse with a target membrane without the bilayer breaking or leaking.

3. Both vesicles bud from the trans face of the Golgi apparatus. Lysosomes are formed by the Golgi apparatus, not by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

4. Formation of the lysosome is budding, not exocytosis, nothing leaves the cell and no vesicle fuses with the cell surface membrane, so the area of the cell surface membrane is unchanged. Membrane is removed from the Golgi apparatus.

5. Release of the glycoprotein is exocytosis: the secretory vesicle fuses with the cell surface membrane, so the vesicle membrane is added to it and the total area of the cell surface membrane increases.

Gap closed: lysosomes bud from the Golgi, not the smooth ER.

Gap closed: budding is not exocytosis. Exocytosis adds membrane to the cell surface membrane; budding removes membrane from the donor organelle.

Gap closed: vesicles fuse because the weak hydrophobic interactions holding the bilayer together make it fluid, so membranes slide and merge instead of tearing.

(c) A bacterium of similar volume secretes a digestive enzyme at a comparable rate, yet has none of the membrane-bound organelles of the cell in (a) and (b). Describe how its genetic material is organised, and explain how it exports the enzyme. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) How a bacterium secretes an enzyme without a nucleolus, rough ER or Golgi apparatus. [4]

1. The bacterium has no nucleus. Its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid (R! nucleus / nucleolus / "genetic material" / "bacterial chromosome" on its own, the structure must be named).

2. The DNA is circular, not associated with histone proteins, and the nucleoid is not enclosed by any membrane / nuclear envelope.

3. It has no nucleolus and no membrane-bound organelles; its ribosomes are 70S and free in the cytoplasm, and translation can begin on an mRNA that is still being transcribed.

4. The enzyme is exported directly across the cell surface membrane by transport proteins, so no transport vesicle, Golgi modification or secretory vesicle is required.

Gap closed: a prokaryote's DNA sits in a nucleoid. Writing "nucleus" is an outright reject.

Sources & concepts

Source: ACJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q1 and HCI Prelim 2025 P2 Q1a(i)/(iii) for the nucleoid marking points and the reject list; the rRNA-to-ribosome chain is the verbatim key to "outline how ribosomes are formed" [4] and to the liver-cell nucleoli question in the school topical bank; the Golgi trans-face budding wording is the verbatim organelle-identification key ("at the trans face, secretory vesicles, Golgi vesicles and lysosomes continuously bud / pinch off"). Membrane-area consequences of budding versus exocytosis: VJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q1(b)(i)/(ii) key. [INFERRED: extension, no official key] the ranking of membrane-area change across the two vesicle fates.

Concepts fused: (1) nucleolus → rRNA → ribosomal subunits → protein synthesis as a causal chain; (2) unequal ribosomal subunits; (3) lysosome origin at the Golgi trans face; (4) budding versus exocytosis and what each does to membrane area; (5) fluidity as the enabling property for vesicle traffic; (6) the typical bacterial cell and the nucleoid.

Question 2 [14 marks]

(a) A graph of the rate of entry of glucose into a cell against the concentration of glucose outside the cell rises steeply, then flattens into a plateau marked X. Four suggestions are made for the cause of the plateau at X.

AAll the carrier proteins are saturated with glucose.
BThe carrier proteins are denatured and no longer able to function.
CThe cell has used up its supply of ATP.
DThe concentrations of glucose inside and outside the cell are equal.

For every option, say whether it is correct and why. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Audit all four suggested causes of the plateau at X. [4]

1. A is correct. All the carrier proteins are saturated / every binding site is occupied, so the rate cannot rise further no matter how much glucose is outside. The number of carrier proteins is now the limiting factor.

2. B is incorrect. Nothing in the experiment changes temperature or pH, so the carriers are not denatured. If they were, the rate would fall towards zero, not hold at a constant maximum.

3. C is incorrect. Glucose entry down its gradient is facilitated diffusion, which requires no ATP. Even in a case that did use ATP, an exhausted ATP supply would collapse the rate, not hold it level.

4. D is incorrect. If the internal and external concentrations were equal there would be no concentration gradient and no net entry, so the line would fall to the x-axis, not plateau at a high rate.

Gap closed: a transport plateau is carrier saturation, not ATP running out.

(b) In Amoeba, a contractile vacuole swells, migrates to the cell surface membrane and fuses with it, expelling excess water; proteins embedded in the vacuole membrane pump ions into its lumen. Explain how the vacuole fills, and identify every distinct transport process named or implied here. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) How a contractile vacuole fills, and every transport process involved. [5]

1. Protein pumps / carrier proteins in the contractile vacuole membrane actively transport ions into the lumen against their concentration gradient, using energy from the hydrolysis of ATP. (R! channel proteins.) "Pump" always means active transport.

2. The solute concentration of the lumen rises, so the water potential of the lumen becomes more negative than that of the cytoplasm. (R! "higher" or "lower" water potential.)

3. Water moves from the cytoplasm, of less negative water potential, into the lumen, of more negative water potential, down the water potential gradient, by osmosis, passing through aquaporins / water channel proteins by facilitated diffusion.

4. The hydrophobic core of the bilayer is impermeable to ions, so the ions accumulate in the lumen and cannot leak back out, which is what holds the water there.

5. Membrane fluidity allows small vesicles to fuse with the vacuole so it can enlarge, and allows the full vacuole to fuse with the cell surface membrane so the water is expelled by exocytosis.

Processes named or implied: active transport (ions in), osmosis (water in), facilitated diffusion (water through aquaporins), exocytosis (water out).

Gap closed: the word "pump" in a stem is an instruction to write active transport.

(c) As the external concentration is raised, the rate of uptake of solute P keeps rising in direct proportion with no upper limit, while that of solute Q rises and then levels off. Deduce the route each takes, and judge why a cell that loses its transmembrane proteins loses more than one transport process. [5]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Deduce the route of P and of Q, and judge the cost of losing transmembrane proteins. [5]

1. P crosses by simple diffusion. The rate is directly proportional to the concentration gradient with no upper limit, because P passes through the phospholipid bilayer itself, no protein is involved and so there is nothing that can become saturated.

2. Q crosses by facilitated diffusion or active transport. The rate levels off because all the channel or carrier proteins become saturated, and their number in the membrane is finite and now limiting.

3. Simple diffusion and osmosis are the only routes that need no membrane protein; every other route depends on one.

4. Transmembrane proteins are not a single class, they include channel proteins, carrier proteins for facilitated diffusion, pumps for active transport, co-transporters, and receptors for cell signalling.

5. Judgement: a cell that loses them loses facilitated diffusion, active transport, co-transport and signal reception all at once, keeping only simple diffusion of small non-polar molecules and osmosis. No other single membrane component carries that many functions, which is why its loss costs most.

Gap closed: simple diffusion does not plateau. Facilitated diffusion and active transport do, because both depend on a finite number of proteins.

Gap closed: transmembrane proteins include the carriers, which is exactly why they are the costliest component to lose.

Sources & concepts

Source: Topical MCQ "What is the cause of the plateau at X?" (a, verbatim stem, all four options and key; the option-by-option audit is an [INFERRED: extension, no official key] rewrite of a one-mark item into four). VJC Prelim P2, contractile vacuole "explain how the structure of the contractile vacuole membrane enables it to perform its function" [4] (b, verbatim key including the rejects on channel proteins and on "higher/lower water potential"; the demand to name every transport process is the extension). Simple-versus-facilitated curve-shape MCQ plus the artificial-membrane question "state the limitations of a membrane made only of phospholipids" (c, verbatim marking points, fused).

Concepts fused: (1) carrier saturation as the cause of a transport plateau; (2) ATP dependence and what its absence would actually look like on a graph; (3) the pump → water potential → osmosis → exocytosis chain of the contractile vacuole; (4) linear versus saturating uptake kinetics as a diagnostic for the route taken; (5) the functional breadth of transmembrane proteins.

Question 3 [13 marks]

(a) A red blood cell is forced through a capillary narrower than its own diameter, then returns to its original shape without leaking. Explain how the cell surface membrane allows this. (Answer in terms of the phospholipid bilayer.) [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How the cell surface membrane allows a red blood cell to deform and recover. [4]

1. The membrane is fluid: the phospholipids and proteins move laterally within their own monolayer.

2. They are held only by weak hydrophobic interactions between the hydrocarbon tails, which are easily broken and re-formed.

3. So the bilayer can change shape and be deformed without breaking, and reseals as the cell resumes its shape, which is why nothing leaks out.

4. Unsaturated hydrocarbon tails carry kinks that prevent close packing, keeping the membrane fluid at body temperature, and cholesterol adds mechanical stability and flexibility so the membrane does not tear under shear.

Gap closed: any stem about stretching, squeezing or deformation is answered with fluidity and lateral movement.

(b) Lipid rafts are patches of membrane that hold a higher proportion of cholesterol and phospholipids with straighter, less kinked hydrocarbon tails than the membrane around them.

Predict how a raft region behaves compared with the membrane around it when the cell is cooled to 5 °C and when it is warmed to 45 °C, and account for both predictions. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Predict raft behaviour against non-raft behaviour at 5 °C and at 45 °C. [4]

At 5 °C:

1. The non-raft region stays relatively fluid, because its kinked unsaturated tails already prevent the phospholipids packing closely.

2. The raft's straight, less kinked tails would pack closely and the region would tend towards a semi-solid / gel state, but the higher proportion of cholesterol inserts between the tails and prevents close packing, so the raft does not solidify and stays workably fluid.

At 45 °C:

3. Increased kinetic energy makes the phospholipids move faster, so the non-raft region becomes markedly more fluid and more permeable.

4. In the raft, the cholesterol restrains the movement of the phospholipids and reduces fluidity, so the raft stays more ordered, more stable and less permeable than the membrane around it, cholesterol also acts as a plug, reducing the escape of ions and small polar molecules.

5. The point of the contrast: cholesterol works in both directions, raising fluidity at low temperature and lowering it at high temperature, whereas unsaturation only ever shifts fluidity one way.

Gap closed: at low temperature cholesterol prevents the chains packing closely, so the membrane does not become semi-solid. Do not invert this.

Gap closed: cholesterol buffers both ways; unsaturation is one-directional. Cholesterol alone also gives mechanical stability and reduced permeability.

(c) Cells suspended in a dilute salt solution stay intact at 25 °C but burst at 55 °C. Give two independent explanations for the bursting. [5]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Two independent explanations for bursting at 55 °C. [5]

Route one, the bilayer.

1. The higher temperature raises the kinetic energy of the phospholipids, so they move laterally and flip between layers more.

2. The weak hydrophobic interactions between the hydrocarbon tails are overcome, the molecules move further apart and gaps open in the bilayer.

3. The membrane becomes more fluid and more permeable, so it can no longer contain the contents and the cell bursts.

Route two, the proteins.

4. Above the optimum, the increased vibration breaks the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions that maintain the 3D conformation of the pumps and carrier proteins, so they are denatured and their binding sites lose their complementary shape.

5. Ions can no longer be pumped out, solutes accumulate, the water potential of the cytoplasm becomes more negative than that of the surrounding solution, water enters by osmosis and, with no cell wall to resist the pressure, the cell bursts.

Gap closed: bursting at high temperature has two independent routes, hydrophobic interactions in the bilayer being overcome, and denaturation of the pump proteins. "Whenever there's temperature, think enzymes" is your own rule; write both.

Sources & concepts

Source: MJC/school topical "explain what is meant by the fluidity of the cell membrane and describe a factor affecting it" and the lens-lipid oxygen-permeability data question (a and c route one, verbatim marking points). VJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q4(b) lipid-raft figure and its two-difference structural question (b, the figure is verbatim; the 5 °C / 45 °C prediction is [INFERRED: extension, no official key] built on the verbatim cholesterol key "increases the stability of membranes / decreases membrane fluidity by restraining the movement of phospholipids at relatively warm temperatures; or increases membrane fluidity by hindering the close packing of phospholipids at low temperatures"). Arctic-fox cholesterol question (b, verbatim). Enzyme-denaturation bond list from the pH/temperature keys in the enzymes bank (c route two, verbatim).

[FIG: q3b_lipidraft.png], Fig. 3.1 is the lipid-raft cross-section from VJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q4(b), page 10, printed there as Fig. 4.2. Raft and non-raft regions bracketed, cholesterol density and tail kinks visible. Extracted and embedded.

Concepts fused: (1) fluidity as the answer to every deformation stem; (2) weak hydrophobic interactions as the reason the bilayer reseals; (3) cholesterol's dual, bidirectional effect set against the one-directional effect of unsaturation; (4) kinetic energy → lateral movement → permeability; (5) denaturation of transport proteins as a separate, sufficient cause of lysis.

Question 4 [18 marks]

(a) Fig. 4.1 shows the four structural levels of β-keratin in a feather.

Feathers are not easily degraded. Rank the four levels by how much each contributes to that, and justify the ranking. [6]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Rank the four levels of β-keratin by contribution to the stability of the fibre. [6]

1. Polypeptide. Antiparallel β-pleated sheets stabilised by numerous intrachain hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N-H groups of neighbouring segments of the same chain.

2. Dimer. Two covalent disulfide bonds between the two β-keratin polypeptides.

3. Fibril. Two covalent disulfide bonds between β-keratin dimers, holding a row of dimers together. (R! peptide bonds.)

4. Fibre. Numerous / extensive disulfide bonds between neighbouring fibrils. ("More" on its own is rejected; the count in one printed segment is ignored, because the figure shows only a fragment of a long fibre.)

5. The ranking. Fibre contributes most, because it carries the largest number of covalent cross-links and they run in every direction, so a break in one place is not transmitted through the structure; then fibril, then dimer, both covalent but with far fewer bonds each; the polypeptide contributes least, because hydrogen bonds are individually weak even though there are many of them.

6. The reason the ranking works at all: disulfide bonds are covalent, therefore strong, and are not overcome by temperature or pH, which is why keratin resists degradation. (R! describing hydrogen bonds as strong bonds.)

Gap closed: a keratin-stability answer has to be broken down level by level, polypeptide, dimer, fibril, fibre, with the bond named at each. A general statement about disulfide bonds is worth one mark, not four.

(b) A tendon, a plant cell wall and a phospholipid bilayer of equal thickness are each pulled until they fail. Rank them by the load each bears before it gives way, and in every case say what it is that gives way. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Rank a tendon, a plant cell wall and a phospholipid bilayer by the load each bears, and say what gives way in each. [8]

Ranking, greatest load first: tendon (collagen) > plant cell wall (cellulose) > phospholipid bilayer.

The plant cell wall, cellulose.

1. Monomer β-glucose, joined by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds with alternate residues inverted, giving long, straight, unbranched chains.

2. The -OH groups project outwards in all directions from each chain, so numerous interchain hydrogen bonds form between the projecting -OH groups of neighbouring chains, cross-linking them into microfibrils and then macrofibrils. Under load it is those interchain hydrogen bonds that give way, not the chains themselves, the covalent backbone survives and the chains slide apart.

The tendon, collagen.

3. Monomer amino acids; three left-handed helical polypeptides wind into a tropocollagen triple helix. (R! tropocollagen as the monomer.)

4. Almost every third residue is glycine, whose R group is a single hydrogen atom. Every third residue passes through the crowded centre of the triple helix, where only an R group as small as glycine's will fit, so the three chains lie close together and coil tightly.

5. Hydrogen bonds are both intrachain, within each helix, and interchain, between the N-H of glycine and the C=O of a residue on a neighbouring backbone, holding the triple helix together.

6. Tropocollagen molecules lie in a staggered arrangement and are joined by covalent cross-links between the C-terminal and N-terminal of adjacent molecules, building fibrils and fibres.

Why the tendon outranks the cell wall.

7. Collagen bears the greater load. Cellulose's only cross-links between chains are hydrogen bonds; collagen has covalent cross-links between tropocollagen molecules on top of its hydrogen bonds, and a covalent bond is individually far stronger than a hydrogen bond. The staggered arrangement spreads the load so no single junction takes all of it. What finally gives way in a tendon is therefore a covalent cross-link, which takes far more force than the hydrogen bonds that fail first in cellulose.

The phospholipid bilayer, last, and by a long way.

8. It is not a long linear macromolecule, the phospholipids are separate molecules not joined to one another by covalent bonds, so there is no continuous chain along which a pulling force can be transmitted. They are held only by weak hydrophobic interactions, which is what makes the bilayer fluid, and a fluid structure has no tensile strength at all. There are no interchain hydrogen bonds cross-linking neighbours into rigid fibres. What gives way is nothing in particular, the molecules simply slide past one another and the layer flows apart, which is why the bilayer fails under a load neither of the other two would notice.

Gap closed: cellulose's tensile strength comes specifically from interchain hydrogen bonding between the projecting -OH groups. Monomer, bond and branching alone do not reach the mark.

Gap closed: collagen beats cellulose because of covalent cross-links between tropocollagen molecules.

Gap closed: collagen hydrogen bonding is intrachain AND interchain, N-H of glycine to C=O of a neighbouring backbone.

Gap closed: every third residue passes through the centre of the triple helix, so crowded that only glycine's R group fits. Say the sentence, do not gesture at "glycine is small".

Gap closed: a phospholipid gives no structural support because it is not a covalently joined linear macromolecule, it is held by weak hydrophobic interactions and so is fluid, and it forms no rigid interchain cross-links.

(c) Two identical samples of a fibrous protein are treated, one with a buffer at pH 2 and one with 70% methanol. Predict the effect of each treatment and account for the difference between them. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Predict the effect of pH 2 and of 70% methanol on a fibrous protein. [4]

1. At pH 2 the excess H⁺ ions change the ionisation / charge of the R groups, -COO⁻ gains H⁺ to become -COOH, and -NH₂ gains H⁺ to become -NH₃⁺.

2. This disrupts the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that maintain the 3D conformation, so the conformation is lost and the protein is denatured.

3. Methanol is amphipathic. Its non-polar portion interacts with the hydrophobic R groups, so it disrupts the hydrophobic interactions holding the non-polar residues together.

4. The difference: pH acts indirectly, through the charge on the R groups, on ionic and hydrogen bonds; methanol acts directly on hydrophobic interactions. Neither breaks disulfide bonds or peptide bonds, both of which are covalent, so a heavily disulfide-cross-linked fibre survives both treatments far better than one held mainly by hydrogen and ionic bonds.

Gap closed: the pH sentence is "disrupt the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that maintain the 3D conformation", reached through pH → ionisation of R groups changes → those bonds disrupted → conformation lost.

Gap closed: an amphipathic solvent such as methanol disrupts hydrophobic interactions, not ionic bonds.

Question 5 [15 marks]

(a) Describe the structure of haemoglobin. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Describe the structure of haemoglobin. [5]

1. Primary. The unique number and sequence of amino acids in each polypeptide, joined by peptide bonds. Haemoglobin has two α-chains and two β-chains, the α and β sequences differing.

2. Secondary. Regular coiling of the polypeptide backbone into α-helices, held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and the N-H of every fourth peptide bond in the main chain. Haemoglobin is almost entirely α-helical, with no β-pleated sheet.

3. Tertiary. Each chain folds further into a specific 3D conformation, held by bonds between R groups within the same chain, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bonds. Hydrophilic R groups face outwards into the aqueous surroundings and hydrophobic R groups are buried in the interior, making the molecule soluble; a hydrophobic cleft in each chain holds the haem group.

4. Quaternary. The four polypeptides associate into one compact globular molecule, held by the same R-group interactions, now acting between chains.

5. Prosthetic group. Each chain carries one haem group, a non-protein iron-containing group with a central Fe²⁺ that binds one O₂; four haem groups, so up to four O₂ per haemoglobin molecule. Haemoglobin is therefore a conjugated protein.

Gap closed: "describe the structure" of a quaternary protein means all four levels plus the prosthetic group. A quaternary summary on its own caps you at about a third of the marks.

(b) A company needs one protein to carry oxygen around the body in an artificial blood substitute. Given only that at 20 mm Hg myoglobin is about 84% saturated and haemoglobin about 20%, decide which of the two to use and justify the choice from their structures. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Choose myoglobin or haemoglobin for an artificial blood substitute, from the 20 mm Hg data and the two structures. [5]

1. Myoglobin consists of one polypeptide chain with one haem group; it has tertiary structure only and no quaternary structure, so cooperative binding is impossible.

2. Its dissociation curve is hyperbolic and it saturates at very low oxygen concentrations, 84% saturated at 20 mm Hg.

3. Haemoglobin's four subunits interact cooperatively: binding of one O₂ molecule to one subunit raises the affinity of the remaining subunits for oxygen, which gives a sigmoidal curve rising sharply only between about 15 and 35 mm Hg, 20% saturated at 20 mm Hg.

4. Higher percentage saturation at the same oxygen concentration means higher affinity, so myoglobin has the higher affinity. A curve lying to the left is higher affinity; a curve shifted to the right is lower affinity.

5. Decision: choose haemoglobin. A carrier must load in the lungs and unload in respiring tissue; myoglobin's affinity is so high that it holds its oxygen until the concentration falls below about 20 mm Hg, which makes it an excellent local store and a poor transporter, an artificial blood built on it would pick oxygen up and never let go of it. Haemoglobin's sigmoidal curve means a small fall in oxygen concentration in the tissues produces a large fall in saturation, so it releases a large fraction of its oxygen exactly where it is needed and reloads fully in the lungs.

Gap closed: myoglobin, one chain, tertiary only, one haem group, no cooperativity, hyperbolic curve, high affinity, excellent store, poor transporter.

Gap closed: a curve shifted right is lower affinity, shifted left is higher affinity. Say it as a rule, not as a guess.

(c) A mutant haemoglobin folds with its hydrophilic residues in the interior. Predict what happens to the molecule inside a red blood cell, and explain why it would fail to carry oxygen even if it did stay in solution. [5]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Predict the fate of a haemoglobin folded with its hydrophilic residues inside, and say why it could not carry oxygen even in solution. [5]

1. Structure: hydrophilic R groups in the interior means hydrophobic R groups are displaced to the surface; the R-group interactions change, so the chain folds into a different 3D conformation.

2. With hydrophobic residues on the outside the molecule is insoluble in the aqueous cytoplasm of the red blood cell. ("Cannot transport" on its own does not earn the structural mark, insoluble is the word.)

3. Prediction: exposed hydrophobic R groups are energetically unfavourable in an aqueous environment, so the molecules cluster with one another and bury their hydrophobic surfaces against each other, shielding them from the water of the cytosol. They precipitate as insoluble aggregates inside the cell.

4. Consequence: the aggregates distort the red blood cell, which may then be destroyed as it passes through capillaries, and the aggregated haemoglobin is no longer free in solution to pick up oxygen at all.

5. Even in solution it would fail, because the hydrophobic cleft in each chain that holds the haem group is built from hydrophobic residues facing inwards. With the interior now hydrophilic the cleft is lost, the haem group cannot be held in place, and there is no Fe²⁺ presented for oxygen to bind to. The altered conformation also disrupts the subunit interactions on which cooperative binding depends.

Gap closed: buried hydrophilic residues earn "insoluble" plus the loss of the hydrophobic cleft for the haem group.

Gap closed: misfolded proteins aggregate because exposed hydrophobic R groups shield themselves from the aqueous surroundings by clustering, not merely because the shape is wrong.

Sources & concepts

Source: RI Prelim P2 Q1(b)(i) "describe the structure of PFK" [4] read across to haemoglobin, with the four-level key verbatim including "most of its hydrophilic amino acid side chains are on the external surface while hydrophobic side chains are buried in the interior" (a). ACJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q3, myoglobin model and the C/D dissociation curves, with the verbatim key including the 84% and 20% data at 20 mm Hg (b, data verbatim; the blood-substitute decision is [INFERRED: extension, no official key]). School structured question "state the effect on haemoglobin's structure for the following defects and how it affects the function", part (ii) "hydrophilic amino acid residues in the interior of structure" [2] (c, verbatim key). The aggregation prediction is [INFERRED: extension, no official key], built from the verbatim collagenase/collagen solubility key and the misfolded-protein key in the proteins bank.

Concepts fused: (1) the four-level description as the standard answer to "describe the structure"; (2) cooperativity as the structural cause of a sigmoidal curve; (3) affinity read off saturation at a fixed oxygen concentration, and the left/right shift rule; (4) store versus transporter as a functional judgement; (5) the prosthetic group and the hydrophobic cleft that holds it; (6) hydrophobic burial as the reason globular proteins are soluble, and its failure as the reason they aggregate.

Question 6 [14 marks]

(a) A graph of the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction against substrate concentration rises steeply from the origin, then flattens. Account for the shape of the curve across its whole range, and predict how the curve would change if the enzyme concentration were doubled. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Account for the whole curve, then predict the effect of doubling the enzyme concentration. [5]

The curve has two regions and each has a different limiting factor. Say both.

1. Initial steep rise, substrate concentration is limiting. There is an excess of enzyme, so not all the active sites are occupied. Raising the substrate concentration increases the frequency of successful collisions between substrate molecules and active sites, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time and the rate rises in proportion.

2. Plateau, enzyme concentration is limiting. All the active sites are occupied / the enzyme is saturated, so the number of active sites, and therefore the enzyme concentration, is now the limiting factor. Further substrate has no effect because each molecule must wait for an active site to become free; the rate is at Vmax.

3. The height of the plateau is set by how fast the enzyme can turn substrate over, not by how much substrate is present.

4. Doubling the enzyme concentration. Twice as many active sites, so Vmax doubles and the plateau sits at twice the height; the curve rises more steeply and levels off at a higher substrate concentration.

5. Km is unchanged, because Km is a property of the enzyme and its substrate, not of how much enzyme is present.

Gap closed: a rate-against-substrate curve is answered in two regions with two different limiting factors, substrate in region 1, number of active sites in region 2. One undivided explanation loses half the marks.

(b) Hexokinase I has a Km of 0.05 mmol dm⁻³ for glucose while liver glucokinase has a Km of 10 mmol dm⁻³, and the two differ at only a small number of amino acid positions. Decide which keeps working in a cell where glucose is scarce, and explain how so few amino acid differences can produce a Km two hundred times larger. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Choose between hexokinase I and glucokinase for a glucose-poor cell, and explain a 200-fold Km difference from a handful of amino acids. [5]

1. Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction proceeds at half of Vmax. The lower the Km, the less substrate is needed to half-saturate the enzyme, so the higher the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

2. Hexokinase I has the far lower Km (0.05) and therefore the far higher affinity; glucokinase has the higher Km (10) and the lower affinity. The higher the Km, the lower the affinity, the two are inverse.

3. Decision: hexokinase I keeps working where glucose is scarce. It can still form enzyme-substrate complexes and run near its maximum rate at low glucose concentration, it phosphorylates glucose even when the concentration in the cell is low, whereas glucokinase needs roughly two hundred times more glucose even to reach half its maximum rate, which is why the liver enzyme only becomes active when blood glucose is high.

4. The amino acids that differ are part of the active site. [Compulsory, without this the chain does not connect. A substitution anywhere that left the active site's conformation untouched would not change Km at all.]

5. The R groups of the differing amino acids have different properties, so the R-group interactions differ, the polypeptide folds differently, and the 3D conformation of the active site differs. A less complementary active site binds glucose less readily, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, the affinity is lower and Km is higher.

Gap closed: Km and affinity are inverse. Higher Km, lower affinity, no exceptions.

Gap closed: a single amino acid substitution only explains a fall in activity if you state that the amino acid is part of the active site. That sentence is the whole mark.

(c) Adding molecule M to an enzyme lowers its rate and more substrate does not restore it, while adding molecule N lowers the rate but more substrate restores it fully. Deduce how each acts, name each type of inhibition, and say which of the two a cell would use to switch a whole metabolic pathway on and off. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Deduce how M and N act, name each, and choose the one a cell would use as a pathway switch. [4]

1. N is a competitive inhibitor. It is similar in structure to the substrate and binds to and blocks the active site so the substrate cannot bind; adding more substrate lets substrate molecules outcompete it for the active site, so the rate is restored. Vmax unchanged, Km increased.

2. M is a non-competitive inhibitor. It does not resemble the substrate in structure and binds at a site other than the active site, causing a change in the 3D conformation of the active site so the substrate can no longer bind. More substrate cannot displace it, so the rate is not restored. Vmax falls, Km unchanged.

3. Name both types explicitly. Describing the mechanism without writing "competitive" and "non-competitive" leaves a mark on the table.

4. The switch: a cell uses the M type, as allosteric inhibition. The inhibitor binds to the allosteric site, a site other than the active site, on a multimeric enzyme, and triggers a change in the 3D conformation of the active sites of all the subunits, stabilising the enzyme in its inactive conformation; an allosteric activator does the converse and stabilises the active conformation. Because the effect cannot be overridden by substrate accumulating, it works as a genuine on/off switch, which is how end-product inhibition regulates a whole pathway. (Do not mix non-competitive inhibition with allosteric inhibition, allosteric describes a multimeric enzyme with a defined allosteric site.)

Gap closed: name the inhibitor type. Describing the mechanism without writing the words "non-competitive" leaves a mark on the table every time.

Gap closed: the allosteric site and the active site are different sites. Binding at the allosteric site changes the shape of the active site, activator stabilises the active form, inhibitor stabilises the inactive form.

Sources & concepts

Source: JJC Prelim P1 urease item, verbatim marking points on what limits the rate at P and at Q (a); the doubling prediction is [INFERRED: extension, no official key]. School structured key "enzyme B has a lower affinity for its substrate / the higher the Km the lower the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate", the hexokinase I key "ref. to high affinity of hexokinase I for glucose; this allows hexokinase I to phosphorylate glucose even when glucose concentrations in the cell are low", and the catalase amino-acid-position key with its compulsory first marking point "amino acid at position 2 is part of the active site of enzyme" (b, all verbatim; the paired Km values are [INFERRED: extension, no official key]). Enzymes-bank reference list R2a/R2b/R3a/R3b, verbatim, including "non-competitive inhibitor does not resemble the substrate in structure", "allosteric inhibitor binds to the allosteric site to trigger a change in the 3D conformation of the active sites of all subunits / stabilise the inactive form of the enzyme. Accept the converse for an allosteric activator" and the instruction "reject mixing of non-competitive inhibition with allosteric inhibition"; the competitive/ non-competitive contrast is the verbatim three-point key "competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration while allosteric inhibition cannot" (c).

Concepts fused: (1) two-region limiting-factor analysis; (2) what changes and what does not when enzyme concentration changes; (3) Km as an inverse measure of affinity and as a basis for a suitability judgement; (4) active-site residues as the link between primary structure and catalytic performance; (5) allosteric versus non-competitive inhibition, and the requirement to name the type.

Question 7 [13 marks]

(a) Draw the reaction that joins two α-glucose molecules, then describe the reverse reaction in full. (Four separate things are credited in the drawing.) [6]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Draw the condensation of two α-glucose molecules and describe the reverse reaction. [6]

The four things credited in the drawing:

1. Name the reaction: condensation.

2. Draw both monomers, two α-glucose pyranose rings side by side, each with CH₂OH on carbon 6 and -OH groups on carbons 1 to 4, with the -OH on carbon 1 below the plane of the ring (that is what makes it α), and the carbons numbered.

3. Label the bond fully: α-1,4-glycosidic bond, drawn as an oxygen bridge between carbon 1 of the first ring and carbon 4 of the second, with the whole bond boxed or circled. (Writing "glycosidic bond" without the α and the 1,4 loses the label mark; a line pointing at the bond rather than a box round it is rejected.)

4. Show the water, one molecule of H₂O released, drawn leaving on a curved arrow.

5. The product is maltose, a disaccharide.

The reverse reaction:

6. Hydrolysis. Breaking of the α-1,4-glycosidic bond between the α-glucose residues, in which one water molecule is added per bond broken, where H is added to carbon atom 1 of one α-glucose monomer and OH is added to carbon atom 4 of the other. An enzyme, maltase, or amylase for the polymer, is required.

Gap closed: the hydrolysis sentence is exact, H to carbon 1, OH to carbon 4, one water per bond, and an enzyme is required. "Each anomeric carbon gets a hydroxyl" is not the mark scheme's sentence.

Gap closed: your own four-item drawing checklist is the mark scheme's own list, name the reaction, draw both monomers, label the bond fully, show the water.

(b) A plant extract gives a negative result with Benedict's solution, yet the plant is known to transport a sugar from its leaves. Using only Benedict's solution, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate, describe how you would show that the sugar is present and explain what happens to the bonds at each stage. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Show that a sugar is present after a negative Benedict's result, and say what happens to the bonds. [4]

1. The negative Benedict's result shows there is no reducing sugar present, so the sugar being transported must be a non-reducing sugar such as sucrose. Testing for the absence of reducing sugar first is what makes the rest of the test valid.

2. Boil a fresh sample of the extract with dilute hydrochloric acid. This hydrolyses the glycosidic bond in the non-reducing sugar, adding one water molecule per bond broken and releasing the monosaccharides, which are reducing sugars.

3. Neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate before testing, because Benedict's solution is alkaline and will not work in acid. [This step is the one most often dropped, and without it the final test fails.]

4. Add Benedict's solution in excess and heat in a water bath. A brick-red precipitate confirms that a reducing sugar has now been produced, so a non-reducing sugar was present in the original extract.

Gap closed: acid hydrolysis then neutralise. Both steps, in that order, before the second Benedict's test.

(c) Glycogen is branched but amylose is not. Explain what must be different about the bond at a branch point and why nothing else would do, then state what the branching achieves for the cell. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) What must be different about the bond at a branch point, why nothing else would do, and what branching achieves. [3]

1. A 1,4 bond joins carbon 1 of one residue to carbon 4 of the next, so it continues the chain in the same line. Only a bond formed at carbon 6 can leave the line of the chain, because carbon 6 sits on the CH₂OH group projecting out of the ring rather than in the ring itself.

2. So the branch point is an α-1,6-glycosidic bond, formed between the -OH groups on carbon 1 of a glucose residue in one chain and carbon 6 of a residue in the other, releasing a water molecule in a condensation reaction catalysed by a branching enzyme.

3. Branching gives many free ends, so many enzyme molecules can act on the same glycogen molecule at the same time and glucose is released rapidly for respiration; it also makes the molecule compact, so more glucose is stored per unit volume.

Gap closed: a branch requires a bond involving carbon 6 specifically, because carbon 6 is the only position that leaves the line of the chain.

Sources & concepts

Source: School structured drawing question "draw the molecular structure of maltose and show how it can be catalysed by maltase to produce glucose molecules" [3] and the condensation-drawing item with its verbatim label requirements (a); TJC Prelim P2 Q2(b) "describe the process of hydrolysis of amylose in starch" [3], verbatim key including "H is added to carbon atom 1 of one α-glucose monomer and OH is added to carbon atom four of the other α-glucose monomer" and "enzyme / amylase is required" (a). The plant-extract test question with the provided reagents, plus the verbatim key on why the absence of reducing sugar must be established first and the verbatim semi-quantitative Benedict's design key "first hydrolyse a sample by boiling with dilute hydrochloric acid and then neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate before testing" (b). Branch-point figure question, verbatim key "α-1,6-glycosidic bond formed; between -OH groups of C1 of a glucose monomer in molecule A and C6 of a glucose monomer in molecule B; release of a water molecule via condensation reaction; catalysed by an enzyme Q" (c).

Concepts fused: (1) condensation drawn to the mark scheme's own four-item standard; (2) the exact hydrolysis sentence, including the enzyme requirement; (3) reducing versus non-reducing sugars and the acid-then-neutralise sequence as bond chemistry rather than recipe; (4) bond position as the structural cause of branching; (5) branching as the structural cause of rapid mobilisation.

Question 8 [12 marks]

(a) A liver cell is deprived of glucose for thirty minutes, and then for three days. Predict which of its two energy stores it draws on in each period, and justify both choices. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which store the liver draws on after thirty minutes and after three days. [4]

1. Thirty minutes, glycogen. It is highly branched, so there are many free ends at which glycogen phosphorylase can act simultaneously, and glucose is released rapidly.

2. The glucose released enters respiration directly, in few steps, so ATP is available quickly; the liver also releases it into the blood to maintain blood glucose concentration. This is the store for immediate demand.

3. Three days, fat. The glycogen store is limited in quantity and would be exhausted. Fat yields roughly twice the energy per gram, because fatty acids are far more reduced, more C-H bonds and proportionately less oxygen per molecule, so a given mass lasts far longer, and there is no practical limit on how much can be stored.

4. Fat could not have served the first period, because it is slow to mobilise, it must be hydrolysed to fatty acids and glycerol, and the fatty acids pass through many oxidation steps before ATP is produced. The two stores answer two different demands, speed and density, which is why the cell keeps both.

Gap closed: answer this one in the molecules, mobilisation rate against energy density. Reasoning through the pancreas and hormones does not reach the marking points.

(b) A liver cell converts a large quantity of its stored glycogen into free glucose but cannot export it. Predict what happens to the cell and explain the mechanism, then say why holding the same quantity of energy as fat would have caused no such problem. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Predict the fate of a cell that hydrolyses its glycogen into glucose it cannot export. [4]

1. Glycogen is one very large molecule built from thousands of glucose residues, so it contributes very few solute particles; most of its hydroxyl groups project into the interior of the helices and hydrogen-bond with one another rather than with water, so it is insoluble and osmotically almost inactive and can be stored in large quantities without appreciably affecting the water potential of the cell.

2. Hydrolysing it releases a very large number of small, soluble glucose molecules, so the solute concentration of the cytoplasm rises sharply.

3. The water potential of the cytoplasm becomes much more negative than that of the surrounding tissue fluid, so water enters by osmosis, moving down the water potential gradient from the less negative to the more negative water potential. Prediction: the cell swells and, having no cell wall to resist the pressure, may burst / lyse.

4. Fat would have caused no such problem. Triglycerides are non-polar and hydrophobic, so they are not in solution at all and carry no water of hydration; stored as droplets they contribute essentially nothing to the solute concentration, and fat carries about twice the energy per gram, so fewer molecules are needed for the same energy in the first place. For the same energy content the osmotic effect runs free glucose > glycogen > fat.

5. The rule underneath all of it: osmotic effect follows the number of dissolved solute particles, not the mass and not the energy content. Polymerising cuts the particle count; being hydrophobic takes the molecule out of the count altogether.

Gap closed: fat beats glycogen on osmotic effect because it is hydrophobic and carries no water of hydration, not merely because it is a large molecule.

(c) A high-amylose rice raises blood glucose more slowly after a meal than a low-amylose rice of the same mass. Account for this at the level of the molecule. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Why a high-amylose rice raises blood glucose more slowly. [4]

1. Amylose is unbranched and joined only by α-1,4-glycosidic bonds; amylopectin is branched, with α-1,6-glycosidic bonds at the branch points.

2. A higher amylose content means a lower amylopectin content in the same total mass, so there are fewer branch points and therefore fewer free ends. (Fewer, not none, an amylose chain still has ends.)

3. Each free end is a point at which amylase can bind and act, so fewer ends means fewer enzyme-substrate complexes forming at any one time and a smaller effective surface for the enzyme. Amylose also coils into tight helices whose hydroxyl groups hydrogen-bond internally, making the chain less accessible to the enzyme.

4. So the starch is hydrolysed to maltose and then glucose more slowly, glucose is absorbed into the blood more slowly, and blood glucose rises more gradually.

Gap closed: the missing link is "more amylose means less amylopectin", and only then fewer branch points → fewer free ends → fewer simultaneous points of attack. And it is fewer free ends, never no free ends.

Sources & concepts

Source: School structured keys on storage polysaccharides, verbatim marking points including "most of the hydrophilic OH groups of the glucose residues project into the interior of the helices and form hydrogen bonds with one another", "they can be stored in large quantities without affecting the osmotic potential of cells" and "branched structure allows many enzymes / large surface area for enzymes to act on it at any one time to release glucose quickly" (a, b, c). The three timeframes in (a), the hydrolysed-glycogen scenario in (b) and the blood-glucose framing in (c) are all [INFERRED: extension, no official key] settings placed on top of verbatim keys; the ranking against fat rests on the verbatim lipid energy-density and hydrophobicity marking points. The amylose/amylopectin structural contrast is verbatim from the school key "the amylose component is unbranched whilst the amylopectin component is branched; the glucose residues in the amylose component are linked by (1→4) glycosidic bonds, whilst the glucose residues in the amylopectin component are linked by both (1→4) and (1→6) glycosidic bonds".

Concepts fused: (1) mobilisation rate against energy density as the reason for two stores; (2) particle count as the determinant of osmotic effect; (3) hydrophobicity removing a molecule from the osmotic ledger entirely; (4) branch density → free ends → simultaneous enzyme attack; (5) reading a composition percentage as a statement about what else is present.

#GapWhere it belongsWhy it is not here

34How viruses challenge the cell theoryBook 4, Genetics of VirusesCluster 3 asked it because the source paper did, but virus structure and the acellular argument are Book 4 content. Re-drill it there, where the capsid, envelope and replication cycle are actually taught.

Add all three to the day-1 retrieval list for the book that owns them, not to this one. Gap 27, the nucleoid, stays in Book 1 and is tested in Q1(c), because the typical bacterial cell is a Core Idea 1 outcome.
